video_title: Currencies Around The World Are Dying | Dominic Frisby
gist: Dominic Frisbee (transcribed Frisbee; title says Frisby) argues gold's 35% 2026 drop is a mid-cycle correction driven by speculative froth, rising real yields and a liquidity squeeze. He keeps a $7-10k end-of-decade target based on unavoidable fiat debasement. He calls UK equities (about 12x vs about 18x for the S&P) a screaming buy, says Bitcoin is entering its 500-day pre-halving buy zone, and favours oil and defensive staples. A long middle stretch is UK social and political commentary with little market content.

insights.claim: Dominic Frisbee told Flying Frisbee readers in January 2026 to take profits in precious metals and rotate into oil, a call that paid off two weeks later when US strikes on Iran sent the oil price higher.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Shows Frisbee rotates tactically out of metals when they go vertical; he concedes the timing was lucky.
insights.quote: it was time to take some of your profits out of precious metals and buy oil

insights.claim: Frisbee's contrarian sell signal for gold: once the run is relentless, every mining stock is rising and people start talking about a return to the gold standard, it is time to take profits.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A sentiment gauge for trimming precious-metals exposure near euphoric tops.
insights.quote: as soon as you start thinking we're about to go back on a gold standard it's probably time to uh take some profits

insights.claim: Frisbee sees strong support for gold in the low $3,000s, because it traded in a range there for a long time and old resistance tends to become support. He says gold has fallen further than he expected.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A level to watch for buying gold: Frisbee calls gold probably a buy in that zone.

insights.claim: Rising real yields hurt gold in 2026: bond yields crept higher while Wall Street's inflation expectations stayed flat, which raised the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no yield.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Watch real yields; if they keep rising, gold stays under pressure, and if they turn down, gold gets relief.

insights.claim: Government bond yields of 5-6% are tempting investors away from gold, and UK gilts now yield about 6%, although Frisbee personally refuses to own government bonds.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: High sovereign yields compete with gold for capital, which helps explain gold's weakness.

insights.claim: In a liquidity crisis gold is sold first because it is so liquid (Frisbee calls it the second most traded future after the S&P), as happened in 2008 and in 2020, while panicking investors run to the US dollar.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Expect gold to fall during forced deleveraging even though it is a crisis hedge, which can create buying opportunities.
insights.quote: when you get a liquidity crisis, it's the first thing that goes

insights.claim: Frisbee thinks the late-November 2026 market bounce is just a relief rally inside an ongoing liquidity squeeze.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: He would not chase the rebound, and he warns markets could still get very messy.

insights.claim: Frisbee says gold fell about 35% during 2026, so the debasement trade failed this year, but over three-to-five years gold has still been a great inflation hedge.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Shows how deep the 2026 drawdown was and why holders with long time frames are staying put.

insights.claim: Frisbee keeps his end-of-decade gold target of $7,000-10,000, roughly two to three times the current price of about $3,600: $7,000 if today's trend simply continues and $10,000 if there is a panic spike.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: An explicit long-term upside target; he treats 2026 as a mid-cycle correction in a bull market that is not over.
insights.quote: Our target is 7 to 10,000. And I see no reason to change that.

insights.claim: Frisbee puts the odds of today's liquidity crisis becoming a solvency crisis at about 25-30%. In that case gold and Bitcoin outperform because neither is anyone else's liability.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Tail-risk sizing: hold assets with no counterparty as a hedge against systemic insolvency.
insights.quote: Then you'll want gold and you'll want Bitcoin because then nobody else's liability

insights.claim: Frisbee's debt framework: over-indebted governments can grow, default or debase their way out. Growth is blocked by high taxes and regulation, and the US cannot default openly, so debasement (a back-door default) is the inevitable path. Default and debasement both favour gold.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: The structural reason he expects fiat money to keep losing value and gold to rise over time.
insights.quote: all roads lead to the printer

insights.claim: Interest costs on government debt now exceed the UK education budget and, as Frisbee understands it, US defence spending. He argues interest costs are what will finally cap further debt growth.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Interest costs crowding out other spending push governments toward printing money, which supports debasement hedges.

insights.claim: Central banks keep buying gold heavily with no sign of slowing, because gold is becoming a strategic asset as the US dollar is increasingly used as a tool of war.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Steady central-bank demand puts a floor under gold and supports Frisbee's long-term bull case.

insights.claim: Frisbee says US mining permits are much easier to get under Trump than under Biden, but a leftward swing in the midterms and Democrats' chances in the next election could tighten regulation again.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Political risk for US miners: the easier permitting window may close after the next election.

themes.theme: Debasement of the pound and dollar

insights.claim: Measured against gold, the pound has lost about 40% since 2020 and the dollar roughly 25%, and since 2000 both have lost more than 90%.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Frames gold as the true benchmark for currency debasement, and the pound is falling faster than the dollar.
insights.quote: since the year 2000, measured against gold, both the pound and the dollar have lost more than 90%

insights.claim: Gold cost about £150 an ounce in 1999 and about £2,800-3,000 now, a roughly 94% loss for the pound measured against gold. By contrast, the host notes the US dollar lost about 45% since 2000 on official CPI.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Official CPI badly understates debasement compared with gold-based measures.

insights.claim: Frisbee estimates that economies lose 7-8% a year to money-supply growth while stated inflation is 3-4%. He argues a currency only seizes up when it loses around 20% a year (panic) or 50% (hyperinflation), so slow debasement can go on for decades.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Expect a gradual grind rather than a sudden collapse, which favours holding debasement hedges for the long term rather than timing a crash.

insights.claim: Frisbee expects the pound and dollar to lose another 90% against gold over roughly the next 25 years, arguing that a 90% fall has already happened and nothing stops another one.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A long-range case for steady allocation to hard assets.

insights.claim: Fiat money is debt-based: about 1% of money is physical currency and 99% is digital debt, so a Volcker-style purge with 20% rates would be too deflationary to attempt now, which locks in the debasement path.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Policymakers cannot credibly fight debasement with very high rates, which supports Frisbee's view that hard assets win in the long run.

insights.claim: Frisbee argues the pound and dollar have survived longer than Austrian economics would predict because of the fintech, payments and banking infrastructure built around them, which creates vested interests that let governments get away with debasement.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Explains why collapse predictions keep failing: network effects give fiat a longer life than expected.

insights.claim: Frisbee agrees with Brent Johnson's dollar milkshake theory and expects the euro and the pound to hit trouble before the dollar does.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A relative-value view: favour the dollar over the euro and pound among fiat currencies.

insights.claim: Frisbee credits Bitcoin with teaching people about debasement: investors come to make money and end up learning how fiat money works.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Growing awareness of debasement among retail investors is a long-term tailwind for hard-asset demand.

insights.claim: Frisbee says that on a per-capita basis the UK has the highest exodus of millionaires in the world: almost as many left last year as from China, which has a population of about 1.5 billion against the UK's 65-70 million.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Capital and talent are leaving the UK, which erodes the tax base and adds to fiscal and currency stress.

insights.claim: Frisbee says more than 50% of the UK population are now net takers from the state. He argues the productive base shrinks as those who can leave do, and the government responds only by raising taxes, giving it a 'real-time lesson in the reality of the Laffer curve'.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A structural fiscal-deficit story that supports his bearish view of the pound and gilts.
insights.quote: they're getting a real-time lesson in the reality of the Laffer curve

insights.claim: Frisbee says UK per-capita GDP is now below Mississippi, which he describes as the poorest US state, and that US salaries are about twice UK salaries for the same job while UK taxes are higher.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: The UK's weak relative position underpins the outflow of talent and capital and Frisbee's view on the pound.

insights.claim: Frisbee frames Britain as Rome and America as Byzantium: the heir that ran for another roughly 500 years but eventually debased its coinage and fell. He argues that if Britain could decline, America can too.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A historical template for long-term US decline and currency debasement, though it plays out slowly.
insights.quote: I see Britain as Rome and America as Baantium

insights.claim: Frisbee argues US federalism checks socialism because people and capital can move to low-tax states such as Florida and Texas, which makes the US situation much better than a European superstate.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Supports a relative preference for US over European assets and for low-tax US states.

insights.claim: Frisbee calls the UK stock market a screaming buy: UK companies trade at about 12 times earnings against roughly 18 for the S&P, and they are lean with little debt.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A value rotation trade: buy UK-listed equities at a large discount to US multiples.
insights.quote: The UK stock market is a screaming buy at the moment.

insights.claim: Many UK-listed companies earn most of their revenue abroad (for example in chemicals), so investors buy international businesses at UK valuations without exposure to UK social problems. American acquirers keep buying UK companies, and UK stocks held up well during the recent global correction.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A takeover premium plus low multiples gives UK equities two ways to win; screen for UK-listed firms with mostly overseas earnings.

insights.claim: Frisbee and the host describe buying UK companies as an arbitrage: US-style businesses at UK-style P/E ratios, often trading about two-thirds below comparable US companies, which makes them cheap takeover targets.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Expect continued US-led M&A in UK small and mid caps.
insights.quote: particularly where they're trading up, you know, two/irds off

insights.claim: UK recruitment firms that place candidates in US jobs are a profitable niche: their costs are UK salaries while their commissions are a share of US salaries, which are about twice as high.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: An example of UK businesses profiting from the UK-US wage gap; look for similar cost-arbitrage niches.

insights.claim: Frisbee's '500 day rule' for Bitcoin: buy 500 days before the halving and sell 500 days after, a roughly 1,000-day hold. November 28 2026 marks about 500 days before the next halving, so he says Bitcoin is entering the buy zone.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A dated entry signal for Bitcoin. He notes the rule worked before all four previous halvings but did not catch exact tops or bottoms.
insights.quote: we're coming into the buy zone for Bitcoin

insights.claim: Frisbee says investors would be 'mad to sell' gold, silver or Bitcoin at current levels, even though his own net worth will take a hit in 2026.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: He is holding through the drawdown and does not want to sell near the lows.
insights.quote: I think you'd be mad to sell down here

insights.claim: Gold and silver miners are down 50% or more, so Frisbee expects brutal tax-loss selling in late 2026 and no proper bid for a while. He sees a possible rally in Q1 2027 as the selling ends, provided gold does not sink too low.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A seasonal trade: accumulate beaten-down miners near year-end and look for a January/Q1 bounce.

insights.claim: Frisbee is a long-term holder of oil: he cites about 10 years of underinvestment and low strategic reserves and inventories, and sees the Iran conflict as exposing that shortfall rather than causing it. He does not expect $50-60 oil to return even after the Hormuz disruption ends.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A structurally higher floor for oil supports energy equities as a long-term holding.
insights.quote: I don't think we go back to 60 or $50 oil

insights.claim: Frisbee sees a case for rotating into defensive consumer staples, as in 2000 when dot-com stocks collapsed, naming Coca-Cola, UK bakery chain Gregs and Heineken.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A defensive rotation trade if tech and AI momentum unwinds.
insights.quote: a bit like in 2000 when dot stocks started collapsing there was a big rotation into defensives

insights.claim: Frisbee sees late November 2026 as a time for capital-preservation mode, and notes himself that when he says this it is often a contrarian sign to buy aggressively. He describes the day's big rebound as driven by news about Jensen Huang (transcribed as 'Jensen Hang').
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: Defensive positioning for now, but he admits his own caution is often a contrarian buy signal.
insights.quote: when I start saying you want to be in capital preservation mode that's often an indicator that you want to be buying everything hand over fist

insights.claim: UK retail natural gas costs about 10 times what US consumers pay, whereas prices were the same in 2008, because the UK banned fracking and now imports fracked gas from the US and Norway, which taps the same fields.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: UK energy policy is a cost burden on UK industry and households, and US LNG exporters benefit.

insights.claim: Frisbee hesitates to recommend natural gas, calling it 'the widow maker', but expects it eventually to catch a bid and go 'bananas' like silver. Europe has already drawn down gas stores materially before winter.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisbee
insights.so_what: A volatile optional upside trade; size small given the widow-maker volatility.
insights.quote: sooner or later natural gas bit like silver, it'll just catch a bid and it'll just go bananas
